_work.title: [Collection of Prayers and Talismans] (Princeton, Third Series no. 471, Sub-Saharan African)
_work.blurb: A collection of 181 loose leaves (362 pages) of Sub-Saharan African Islamic manuscript material, 1800–1999 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Third Series no. 471). The leaves are housed between two pieces of animal skin and show significant damage from rodents and insects in the early folios. The manuscript contains prayers, invocations, descriptions and instructions for the use of talismans, amulets, and magic squares — the standard content of West African Islamic protective and divinatory manuscript practice known in the scholarship as the Qur'anic talisman tradition (kitab or hirz tradition). This tradition, widespread from Senegal through Mali, Niger, Nigeria, and across the Sahel, involves copying Qur'anic verses, divine name combinations, and wafq (magic square) grids onto paper (or leather, metal, cloth) as protective charms worn on the body or placed in the home. The Princeton collection preserves 181 separate leaves — not a bound codex but a cache of individual talisman pages — written in a bold, large-format West African Sudanic Arabic script characteristic of the Saharan and Sub-Saharan Islamic manuscript tradition. One leaf shows a remarkable full-page wafq magic square in a distinctive Sub-Saharan African style: a bordered grid with diagonal cross-hatching lines creating X-shaped subdivisions within each cell, and red (or orange-brown) Arabic text filling the triangular sub-cells. This visual formula — the cross-hatched wafq — is specific to West African talismanic manuscripts and is not found in Middle Eastern Islamic MS traditions.

entries.title: Sub-Saharan African Wafq Magic Square with Cross-Hatched Grid (Princeton 3rd Ser. 471, f. 146b)
entries.summary: A full-page wafq (magic square / talismanic grid) in the distinctive visual style of West African Sub-Saharan Islamic manuscript tradition, from a Princeton collection of 181 loose-leaf Sub-Saharan talismanic pages (Third Series no. 471). The grid is a bordered square divided into cells by black ruled lines, with each cell further subdivided diagonally with cross-hatching lines that create X-shaped or four-triangle subdivisions within each cell. Red or ochre-colored Arabic text — Quranic verses, divine names, or magical number sequences — fills each triangular sub-cell. A Bismillah (In the name of God) formula and other Arabic text appears above the grid; similar text (possibly a usage instruction or invocation) appears below. This cross-hatched wafq format — where each main cell is further divided into triangular sub-compartments by diagonal lines — is a specific visual formula of the West African Islamic talismanic tradition (the 'Sudanic' wafq style) that is not found in standard Middle Eastern Arabic or Persian MS traditions. It combines the mathematical structure of the Islamic wafq (magic square, in which rows/columns sum to the same value) with a geometric subdivision pattern that creates a visually denser, more complex talisman surface. The use of red ink for the text against the black-ruled grid creates a high-contrast visual effect that would have made the talisman visually legible even at small size when worn on the body. The leaf belongs to a cache of 181 loose talisman leaves collected in Sub-Saharan Africa, providing a rare documented example of the individual talisman page in the West African protective manuscript tradition.
